t.7.15.1: Then, seeing those Yakṣas fleeing by hundreds of thousands, the Lord of Wealth himself went forth toward the battle.
t.7.15.2: There a Yakṣa named Māṇicāra, exceedingly hard to conquer, surrounded by four thousand Yakṣas, joined battle.
t.7.15.3: Striking them in battle with maces, clubs, darts, spears, lances and hammers, those Yakṣas rushed upon the Rākṣasas.
t.7.15.4: Then, in that battle, a thousand were slain by Prahasta, and another thousand were killed by Mahodara with his mace.
t.7.15.5: And then, O Rāma, the enraged and evil-minded Mārīca struck down two thousand in the mere space of a twinkling of an eye.
t.7.15.6: Having engaged Dhūmrākṣa in the great battle, Māṇibhadra was struck on the chest in anger with a club, yet he did not tremble.
t.7.15.7: Then the Rākṣasa Dhūmrākṣa, struck on the head by Māṇibhadra, who had whirled his mace, fell down reeling.
t.7.15.8: Seeing Dhūmrākṣa struck down, fallen and drenched in blood, the ten-faced one, greatly enraged, rushed at Māṇibhadra.
t.7.15.9: As he rushed forward in fury, like the fire risen at the end of an age, the bull among Yakṣas struck him with three spears.
t.7.15.10: Then he was struck in battle with a mace by the king of the Rākṣasas, and by that blow his crown was knocked to one side. From that time on that Yakṣa has been known as Pārśvamauli.
t.7.15.11: When that great-souled Yakṣa Māṇibhadra had turned away in retreat, O Rāma, a tremendous uproar swelled upon that mountain.
t.7.15.12: Then from afar the Lord of Wealth was seen, bearing his mace, accompanied by Śukra and Proṣṭhapada, and surrounded by Śaṅkha and Padma.
t.7.15.14: Though you are being restrained by me, you do not understand, O wicked-minded one. Later, having reaped the fruit of this, you will know it when you have gone to hell.
t.7.15.13: Seeing his brother on the battlefield, his dignity lost because of a curse, the wise one spoke words befitting the lineage of the Grandsire.
t.7.15.15: For the man who, out of delusion, drinks poison and does not understand what he has done, that deluded one comes to know the fruit of his deed only when it takes its effect.
t.7.15.17: He who shows contempt for his mothers, fathers, brothers and teachers sees the fruit of that when he has fallen into the power of the king of the departed.
t.7.15.16: For the deities rejoice in someone who is endowed with dharma, the one by whom you have been brought to such a condition, and yet you do not understand this.
t.7.15.18: For he who, while the body is impermanent, does not acquire the merit of austerity, that deluded one is tormented afterward, when, having died, he sees his own fate.
t.7.15.20: Intelligence, beauty, strength, wealth, sons, and greatness too: all of this men obtain through the deeds of their former lives, done by themselves.
t.7.15.19: For in no evil-minded person does right understanding arise merely at will; whatever kind of deed one performs, that kind of fruit one reaps.
t.7.15.22: Having spoken thus, he then struck down his ministers, and all of them, led by Mārīca, turned their faces away and fled in every direction.
t.7.15.21: Thus you, whose mind is of such a kind, are bound for hell. I shall not speak with you, a man of wicked conduct; this is my resolve.
t.7.15.23: Then Daśagrīva, struck on the head with a mace by that great-souled lord of the Yakṣas, did not waver from his place.
t.7.15.24: Then, O Rāma, those two, striking each other with furious blows in that supreme battle, became neither bewildered nor weary.
t.7.15.25: Then Dhanada released the fiery weapon of Agni in battle; Daśagrīva warded off that weapon with the weapon of Varuṇa.
t.7.15.26: Then the lord of the Rākṣasas, having entered into Rākṣasa magic, whirled his mighty mace and struck Dhanada on the head.
t.7.15.27: Thus struck by him, the lord of wealth, reeling and drenched in blood, fell down like an aśoka tree whose roots have been cut.
t.7.15.29: Then, O Rāma, having conquered Dhanada, the lord of the Rākṣasas seized his aerial chariot Puṣpaka, the emblem of victory.
t.7.15.28: Then the treasures Padma and the others carried the lord of wealth to the Nandana grove, and there Dhanada was revived by them.
t.7.15.31: Having vanquished the god Vaiśravaṇa, the king mounted that chariot, which moved at will and had been won by his valour, and descended from Kailāsa.
t.7.15.30: It was set with golden pillars, had archways of vaiḍūrya gems, was covered with nets of pearls, and held trees bearing fruits that granted every desire.
